answer: Across 44 quarterly readings of bank new-car loan rates from August 2015 to May 2026, the 72-month rate averaged only 0.1 point above the 60-month rate (median 0.115); it was at least half a point higher in just 1 reading and actually lower in 14. In May 2026 it was lower: 6.97% versus 7.14%. On $35,000 that means $596.21 a month instead of $695.36, and $1,206 more interest in total ($7,927 vs $6,721). Stretching the term at the same rate alone adds $1,412; at the average premium the rate itself adds only $118 of a $1,530 total. History, not a forecast.
guess: Car buyers are commonly told longer loans carry rates 0.5 to 1 point higher, so they would guess the 72-month loan's extra cost comes largely from a worse rate.
changesDecision: At banks the longer term barely changed the rate, so the real price of the lower payment is the extra time paying interest (about $1,200-1,500 on $35,000). The viewer can compare that dollar figure directly with the monthly payment relief, instead of rejecting or accepting 72 months on the belief that the rate is much worse.

assumptions: Loan amount $35,000, level monthly payments, no fees, no prepayment, no trade-in or negative equity rolled in.
Bank survey rates stand for what a typical borrower is offered; dealer/captive financing and credit-score tiers are not modeled.
Latest paired observation (May 2026) used for the dollar example; the average premium example adds the 2015-2026 mean premium to the latest 60-month rate.
limits: History, not a forecast. The survey reports the most common rate at commercial banks once a quarter; it does not cover dealer, captive-finance or credit-union loans, used cars, or borrowers with weak credit, where the term premium may differ. Does not measure depreciation or the risk of owing more than the car is worth on a longer loan.
